newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS-Britain unlikely to join EMU in 1999 - Blair.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Britain unlikely to join EMU in 1999 - Blair.

text.p: Britain's new Labour government said on Wednesday that while it was formally sticking to its "wait-and-see" policy on a single European currency, it was highly unlikely to join at the planned start in 1999.

Separately, Bank of England Deputy Governor Howard Davies said the row in Germany over revaluing Bundesbank gold reserves and the left's victory in the French elections had raised new uncertainty about the outlook for the project.
"It is highly unlikely that Britain would want to join the first wave of monetary union," Prime Minister Tony Blair told parliament.
He also said it would be better for economic and monetary union (EMU) not to go ahead at all than for it to start with "fudged" economic convergence criteria.
Under the Maastricht Treaty on European Union, countries wishing to join a single currency must satisfy requirements on their budget deficits, government debt, interest rates and exchange rates.

"We have always said that the criteria for monetary union should not be fiddled or fudged or botched in any way and if they are, then the answer is not to delay, the answer is not to proceed," Blair said.
Chancellor of the Exchequer (finance minister) Gordon Brown said earlier that the government's position on a single European currency was unchanged.
It would maintain its "wait-and-see" stance while acknowledging that there were big obstacles to joining in the first round.
Brown also unveiled a new employment plan for Europe and promised to make jobs a central theme of Britain's presidency of the European Union in the first half of 1998.

The plan, to be presented to EU finance ministers this weekend, aims to cut unemployment and increase labour market flexibility. It also proposes a taskforce to help smaller firms create jobs and to push for completion of the single market.
Brown said his plan, which he described as the first EU initiative by a British administration for 10 years, did not signal a willingness to give up Britain's veto over key issues.
Debate about the future of the European Union had been focussed too narrowly on the single currency, the euro, and should be broadened to include jobs.

"Better education and higher skills, combined with reduced burdens on business, are the way to guarantee...high and stable levels of growth and unemployment," Brown said. "This is the new economic agenda."

Davies, who will shortly leave the Bank of England to head a strengthened Securities and Investment Board, said the row in Germany over Bundesbank gold and the French election result had introduced new uncertainty about the outlook for EMU.
"It is clear that new elements of uncertainty have entered the scene, making it harder than ever to forecast the outcome next year," he told a financial conference.

The German government has been forced to back down after attempting to revalue the Bundesbank's gold reserves. This would have increased the profits which the central bank pays to Bonn and helped it meet the EMU criteria.
Davies said foreign exchange markets appeared to have become "more persuaded that the euro will begin, but that it will be a broader and possibly weaker euro.

"Very recently, a few doubts seem to have emerged about the project itself, though it would seem that, according to the market, the most likely outcome remains that a euro of some sort would start on time," he said.
The bank's advice remained that it was prudent for businesses to plan on the assumption that the euro would start on January 1, 1999 as planned.
